title: Let Whoever Weeps Weep for God’s Messenger
intro: The Abbasid poet Abu al-Atahiya opens this poem on worldly attachment by mourning the Prophet Muhammad and recalling the traces of his life in Mecca and Medina. Grief gives way to a reckoning with greed and the claims of the poor, in which the poet counts himself among those at fault. He then addresses death before asking a listener to picture the people he will leave behind. Osama Al-Waaedh recites all twenty-six verses of poem 450 in Shukri Faisal’s edition. The earlier Beirut edition begins this poem at “We leaned on this lowly world”, where mourning gives way to admonition.

translation: Let whoever weeps weep for God’s Messenger,
and never forget the grave that lies in Medina.
1.sharh: He calls on anyone who knows grief to mourn the Prophet. The appeal then passes from all who weep to a single listener, asked to hold one grave in mind.

translation: May God reward Muhammad with every good on our behalf.
He was rightly guided, and he guided others.
2.sharh: His prayer speaks for a community in debt to the Prophet. The paired words for guidance distinguish the gift Muhammad received from what he gave to others.

translation: Remembrance can never carry all that he deserves
if you forget that righteous, pure man.
3.sharh: Remembrance is pictured as something that travels, carrying word of the Prophet’s worth. It cannot do him justice if the people who should pass it on have forgotten him.

translation: Can you forget God’s Messenger, the best who walked the earth,
when his traces still endure in the two mosques?
4.sharh: The two mosques give the listener public places in which to remember a life. People still gather to worship where the Prophet himself worshipped.

translation: He was the kindest of all people to everyone,
the noblest of them in house, mountain pass and valley.
5.sharh: His kindness goes out to everyone. The second half traces his origins outwards from his household to the pass and valley that held his people.

translation: After the Prophet Muhammad,
God’s peace be upon him, all that was clear grew clouded.
6.sharh: He breaks off after Muhammad’s name to invoke peace on him. The Arabic holds back the subject, “what was clear”, until after that prayer, when the full extent of the loss comes into focus.

translation: How many beacons he made plain to us,
how many landmarks have since faded away.
7.sharh: A traveller relies on visible signs to find the way. The poet imagines people losing their bearings as the guidance once clear to them fades from their lives.

translation: After him we leaned on this lowly world,
and our appetites laid our faults bare.
8.sharh: With “we”, he shares responsibility for the change he has mourned. The Arabic words for “world” and “lowly” sound strikingly alike.

translation: Every day a lesson is hurled at us.
We see it and only go further down the same road.
9.sharh: The warnings have the force of things thrown at a person. They see each warning clearly and still persist in the conduct it should have stopped.

translation: We delight in a home that has left us nursing grudges
over it, a home that has made us enemies.
10.sharh: Both mentions of “home” mean this world. He traces its legacy from the grudge people nurse within to the hostility that comes out between them.

translation: If someone puts on no clothes of reverence for God,
he goes about naked, however well clothed.
11.sharh: The image recalls the Qur’an’s “garment of reverence”. A man can dress his body completely and still have nothing to cover the faults in his conduct.

translation: Brother, give up hope of favours from people,
every one of them. Set your hope on God all your life.
12.sharh: The hope he asks his brother to give up is the expectation of getting what other people own. He asks his brother to place that hope in God for the rest of his life.

translation: Do you not see that God suffices for his servants?
God alone is enough for them.
13.sharh: The first half asks the listener to recognise who meets his needs. The second repeats the assurance in words built around the idea of having enough.

translation: For many a fault you have laid hands on
in others, you might as well have touched vipers.
14.sharh: A defect of character becomes something the hand can encounter. The comparison makes the cost of depending on another person painfully physical.

translation: Brother, my stinginess and yours keep either of us
from sharing what we have with someone in need.
15.sharh: Having warned his brother about the harm people do, he names a harm the pair of them do themselves. His own meanness comes first in the admission.

translation: We both have full bellies and clothes for all to see,
while others go hungry from evening to morning.
16.sharh: The accusation rests on visible things, a well-fed body and ample clothing. Beside that comfort he sets the long interval someone else spends without a meal.

translation: We live as though made to last. Who among us,
however many years he is granted, will not perish?
17.sharh: Their unwillingness to part with what they own makes sense only if they can keep it for ever. He tests that assumption against the longest life anyone could be given.

translation: Death will have it no other way. Everyone who dwells
on earth must meet it, wherever they may be.
18.sharh: Death has a will and keeps every appointment. The word for someone settled in a place recalls the abiding grave in the opening line.

translation: You cut our hopes short, Death, with a cruel cut.
And you, Death, taught the mourning women how to weep.
19.sharh: He turns to face death and calls it by name in each half of the verse. The mourning women learn how to weep from the very power that gave them cause for grief.

translation: You tore us apart, Death, and scattered us.
You made us know, Death, the calamities you bring.
20.sharh: What is torn is also the company of the living, once held together by the people it has lost. Addressing death twice makes the charge personal in both halves of the line.

translation: You who have been heedless so long, you wake heedless still,
still deluded, still busy with distractions.
21.sharh: The reproach turns from death to someone who goes on ignoring it. Three repetitions of the verb for reaching morning make this sound like a daily routine.

translation: Do we meet a funeral every day
and every day hear someone announce a death?
22.sharh: He sets the sight of a funeral beside the sound of someone bringing the news. Even people who turn away from one reminder are reached by the other.

translation: Every day, because of you, we pity someone wailing.
Every day we join someone in tears.
23.sharh: Those who hear a cry of grief become participants in the mourning. The last verb has an old sense of helping a mourner by joining in the lament.

translation: You there, building beyond what will see you through,
you build for the ruin that time will bring.
24.sharh: The builder has gone beyond what he needs to get through life. Ruin is phrased as the purpose of his building, giving the eventual fate of the house the force of an intention.

translation: You have been gathering for the day your life runs out,
strutting, boastful, showing off.
25.sharh: He piles up possessions while the time in which he can enjoy them runs down. The parade of words for pride makes visible the man who wants others to admire what he owns.

translation: It is as though you had already turned from all you see
and those you left behind had ceased to grieve for you.
26.sharh: He asks the listener to picture his own absence as an accomplished fact. The final word belongs to those left behind and to the day when even their grief for him has eased.

1.1.1.head: بَكى
1.1.1.meaning: To weep for or mourn someone. The Messenger is the one mourned. The call to weep is addressed to anyone capable of it.

1.2.4.head: المَدينَة
1.2.4.meaning: Medina, the city in the Hijaz to which Muhammad emigrated and where he was buried.

1.2.5.head: ثاوٍ
1.2.5.meaning: Abiding or dwelling in a place. The description of the grave calls to mind the one who rests in it.

2.1.6.head: مُحَمَّد
2.1.6.meaning: Muhammad, the Prophet of Islam, for whom the speaker asks God’s blessing on behalf of his community.

2.2.3.head: مَهدِيّ
2.2.3.meaning: Rightly guided. Its active counterpart, hadi, describes someone who guides others.

2.2.4-6.meaning: “And he guided others.” Ibn Rajab gives the wording heard here. Faisal prints “a guide and one who led the way”.

3.1.2.head: سَرى
3.1.2.meaning: To travel or spread, originally to journey by night. Remembrance is imagined as moving among people.

3.2.3.head: بَرّ
3.2.3.meaning: A righteous and beneficent person. The word describes the Prophet. A different first vowel gives the abstract noun for goodness.

3.2.4.head: مُطَهَّر
3.2.4.meaning: Purified, kept free of defilement. The passive form is a second description of the Prophet.

4.2.2.head: المَسجِدان
4.2.2.meaning: Al-Masjidan, the two mosques, are the Sacred Mosque in Mecca and the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina.

4.2.4.head: هِيَ
4.2.4.meaning: “They”, referring to the traces. The final vowel of hiya is prolonged to carry the rhyme.

5.2.2.head: بَيت
5.2.2.meaning: A household or lineage. It is the first in a succession of expressions for the Prophet’s origins.

5.2.3.head: شِعب
5.2.3.meaning: A mountain pass or ravine, here part of the landscape of Mecca. Shi'b differs from sha'b, a people.

7.1.3.head: مَنار
7.1.3.meaning: A beacon or waymark set up to guide travellers.

7.2.2.head: عَلَم
7.2.2.meaning: A conspicuous landmark by which someone can find the way.

7.2.5.head: عافٍ
7.2.5.meaning: Effaced, worn away, said of a trace or an abandoned site.

8.1.1.head: رَكَنَ
8.1.1.meaning: To lean on something, feel secure in it and come to depend on it.

8.1.4.head: دَنِيَّة
8.1.4.meaning: Lowly or base. Daniyya closely echoes dunya, the word for this world immediately before it.

8.2.4.head: مَساوِئ
8.2.4.meaning: Faults or vices. The word also occurs with a final glottal stop. The form heard here gives the poem its usual y-rhyme.

9.2.5.head: تَمادٍ
9.2.5.meaning: Persisting in a course of action, here going further in wrongdoing.

10.1.4.head: تَضاغُن
10.1.4.meaning: Mutual resentment, each person harbouring a grudge against another.

10.2.4.head: تَعادٍ
10.2.4.meaning: Mutual enmity. The next stage of a grudge is to treat the other person as an enemy.

11.1.5-7.head: ثِياب التُّقى
11.1.5-7.meaning: “Clothes of reverence for God” recalls the Qur’an’s “garment of reverence” in 7.26. Clothing gives moral protection a visible shape.

11.2.5.head: كاسٍ
11.2.5.meaning: Clothed, wearing enough to cover the body.

13.2.1.head: حَسب
13.2.1.meaning: Sufficiency. The expression means that God is all his servants need.

14.1.3.head: هَنَة
14.1.3.meaning: Something left unnamed, often a fault, disagreeable trait or hurtful deed.

14.2.6.head: أَفعى
14.2.6.meaning: A viper, a venomous snake. Touching one gives the comparison its sense of immediate danger.

15.2.2.head: فاقَة
15.2.2.meaning: Want or poverty, a lack of what one needs to live.

15.2.5.head: مُؤاسٍ
15.2.5.meaning: Someone who shares what they have with a person in distress. The help in question is material.

16.1.2.head: بَطين
16.1.2.meaning: Large-bellied. The well-fed body makes a visible contrast with the hungry one.

16.1.5.head: كُسوَة
16.1.5.meaning: Clothing or a set of clothes. The plural points to the garments these two visibly possess.

16.2.6.head: طاوٍ
16.2.6.meaning: Hungry, going without food. The image is of a belly drawn in on itself.

18.1.7.meaning: To dwell or settle somewhere. Wherever someone makes a home, death can find them.

18.2.3.meaning: All together, without a single exception.

19.1.1.head: حَسَمَ
19.1.1.meaning: To cut off decisively, putting an end to something.

19.2.1.head: عَلَّمَ
19.2.1.meaning: To teach. The recording sounds like a second l in the place of m. Both printed editions have “you taught”, naming the women who learn and the weeping they learn from death.

19.2.5.head: باكِيَة
19.2.5.meaning: A woman who weeps. The plural here refers to women mourning their dead.

20.1.4-5.head: كُلَّ مُمَزَّق
20.1.4-5.meaning: “Utterly asunder”, a phrase repeating the verb for tearing to express the thoroughness of the scattering.

20.2.5.head: داهِيَة
20.2.5.meaning: A grievous calamity or overwhelming misfortune.

21.2.4.head: لاهٍ
21.2.4.meaning: Distracted, absorbed in diversions. The reciter says lakiya with a k. The diwan has lahiya, which completes the sequence of heedlessness, self-deception and distraction.

22.2.6.head: ناعٍ
22.2.6.meaning: Someone who announces a death, bringing the news aloud to others.

23.1.5.head: رَثى
23.1.5.meaning: To feel compassion for someone, with the preposition li. The consonant sounds close to f in the recording. Both printed texts have th, the sound in “thin”.

23.1.6.head: مُعوِل
23.1.6.meaning: Someone crying aloud in grief, a mourner whose wailing can be heard.

23.2.5.head: أَسعَدَ
23.2.5.meaning: To assist, here by joining someone in lamentation as a sign of sympathy.

24.1.5.head: بَلاغ
24.1.5.meaning: What suffices to carry someone to a destination, such as provisions for a journey. Here it is the shelter needed for a lifetime.

25.2.4.head: مُباهٍ
25.2.4.meaning: Showing off, vying with others in the things one prides oneself on.

26.2.5.head: سالٍ
26.2.5.meaning: Someone whose grief or longing has eased with time.
